source: Turney (2006) Similarity of Semantic Relations (Computational Linguistics 32(3); arXiv cs/0608100)
finding: Defines relational similarity (correspondence between relations of two word pairs) versus attributional similarity (correspondence between properties of two words). Proposes Latent Relational Analysis (LRA): represent a word pair by counts of automatically mined joining patterns in a large web corpus, smooth with SVD, compare pairs by cosine.
numbers: LRA matrix: 17,232 word-pair rows x 8,000 pattern columns, density 5.8%; 4,000 patterns kept; SVD to k=300; corpus about 5x10^10 words (Waterloo MultiText); run time almost nine days for 374 questions on one desktop CPU plus a 16-CPU cluster for the phrase search.
quote: Relational similarity is correspondence between relations, in contrast with attributional similarity, which is correspondence between attributes.
limits: Needs a terabyte-scale searchable corpus. Very slow. The title in our SUBFIELDS row says 'via Wikipedia' but the paper itself used the WMTS web corpus, not Wikipedia.
agent_relevance: This is the founding recipe for cheap relational similarity: a pair becomes a count vector over relation-pattern types and similarity is a cosine. Same idea as our 'count vector of relation types' first pass for far-analogue retrieval.

source: Turney (2006) LRA on 374 SAT analogy questions, Table 12/14
finding: LRA reaches human-average level on SAT verbal analogies and beats lexicon-based and attributional methods by a clear margin.
numbers: LRA 210 correct, 160 wrong, 4 skipped of 374: precision 56.8%, recall 56.1%, F 56.5%. Veale (2004, WordNet paths) 42.8%. Best attributional measure 35.0%. Random 20.0%. Always pick highest co-occurrence 11.8% (significantly below chance); lowest co-occurrence 16.8%. Average US college applicant about 57%; 95% binomial CI for LRA recall 51.0 to 61.2, so human level (57%) is inside it. LRA vs Veale and vs attributional: p<0.05 Fisher exact.
limits: 374 questions, so a 95% interval is about +/-5 points. Human 57% is an estimate from the 78-question verbal SAT, and Claman (2000) says analogy items may be harder, so the human mean may be overstated.
agent_relevance: A pure text-statistics cosine gets to the average-human level on the classic verbal-analogy test. Shows what 'cheap similarity' can do and where its ceiling sat in 2006 (about 56%).

source: Turney (2006) attributional similarity measures on the same SAT questions, Table 4
finding: Word-level (attributional) similarity cannot solve relational questions. All lexicon-based and hybrid WordNet measures stay between 28.5 and 35 percent.
numbers: F scores: Hirst-St-Onge 33.4, Jiang-Conrath 28.5, Leacock-Chodorow 32.0, Lin 29.1, Resnik 34.4, Turney (2001) PMI-IR corpus-based 35.0; VSM relational 47.4; random 20.0. All above chance by Fisher test.
limits: The attributional baselines were run by summing word-to-word similarity of A-C and B-D, a simple reduction; a stronger attributional combiner might do a little better.
agent_relevance: Evidence that surface/word similarity is a weak proxy for relational match. Retrieval keyed on topic words will miss relational analogues; a relation-type vector is needed.

source: Turney (2006) LRA vs VSM and ablations, Tables 14-17
finding: Each of LRA's three additions to the earlier VSM helps, but only synonym substitution gives a significant drop when removed. Corpus size matters.
numbers: VSM-AltaVista (corpus 5x10^11 words) recall 47.1%, 5 skipped; VSM-WMTS (5x10^10) recall 38.5%, 34 skipped; LRA 56.1%, 4 skipped. Ablation recall: no SVD 53.5 (drop not significant), no synonyms 49.5 (22 skipped; significant), neither 47.6 (approx). Interpretability test: need top 300 of 8,000 pattern features before accuracy matches full vector (N=100: 47.6 recall; N=300: 51.3; N=1000: 52.9; N=3000: 55.3).
limits: Ablation sample is only 374 questions; author says the SVD effect is probably real but untestable at this size. 'Without synonyms' mostly fixes sparse data (skipped questions).
agent_relevance: Sparse data is the main failure of count-vector similarity; smoothing and word substitution fix it. Meaning sits spread over the whole vector, so one cannot read off 'the relation' from a few features: an explanation layer must be separate.

source: Turney (2006) noun-modifier relation classification, Tables 20-21
finding: Relational similarity used as the distance in 1-nearest-neighbour classifies noun-modifier pairs into relation classes better than chance but far from solved.
numbers: 600 pairs (Nastase and Szpakowicz 2003). 30 classes: LRA accuracy 39.8% (239/600), F 36.6; VSM-AV 27.8% (167), VSM-WMTS 24.7%; chance F about 3.3. 5 classes: LRA 58.0% (348/600), F 54.6; VSM-AV 45.7%, VSM-WMTS 44.0%. LRA gains significant (Fisher, paired t-test at 95%).
limits: About 20 examples per class; label scheme is one of several; author says more labelled data and a different scheme could change results. No tuning for this task.
agent_relevance: Cheap vectors give a coarse relation label (5 classes at 58%) but not a fine one (30 classes at 40%). Use such vectors for coarse routing, not as a verdict on which relation holds.

source: Turney and Littman (2005) Corpus-based learning of analogies and semantic relations (Machine Learning 60; arXiv cs/0508103)
finding: First VSM for verbal analogy. Each word pair A:B is a vector of 128 log-transformed frequencies (64 joining terms like 'X for Y', 'X of the Y', in both orders) from AltaVista hit counts; analogy score is cosine between pair vectors.
numbers: 374 SAT questions: 176 correct, 193 wrong, 5 skipped. Precision 47.7%, recall 47.1%, F 47.4% (p<0.0001 vs 20% chance). Needed 287,232 AltaVista queries (374 x 6 pairs x 128), about 17 days with a 5 s delay. Log(x+1) weighting was better than raw frequencies.
limits: Hand-written 64 patterns; dependent on one search engine that no longer supports this use. Equals the 2003 ensemble of 13 modules.
agent_relevance: Shows the minimal viable relation embedding: a few dozen relational connector phrases already carry enough signal to beat chance by 27 points.

source: Turney and Littman (2005) precision/recall control and analogy generation
finding: The cosine margin (best cosine minus second best) tells you when the guess is likely right. Thresholding it trades recall for precision. A harder test, picking the match among 369 candidates, shows weaker generation than recognition.
numbers: Margin threshold +0.11: precision 59.2%, recall 11.2%. Threshold -0.11 (two guesses): recall 61.5%, precision 34.5%. Example item traffic:street: best water:riverbed cosine 0.69265, runner-up car:garage 0.68757, margin 0.00508. 369-way choice: correct in top 1 for 31 (8.4%), top 10 for 109 (29.5%); chance for top 10 is 2.7%. Estimated percentile rank of the 47% score: 29 +/-3 (College Board table); a 57% score maps to about the 88th percentile.
limits: Margin rule tuned on the same 374 items. Many 'wrong' top-10 answers in the 369-way test are legitimate analogies (aluminum:metal for barley:grain), so 29.5% underestimates quality.
agent_relevance: A cosine margin is a free confidence signal that code can compute without asking a model, matching our rule that code, not the model, decides. Abstain when the margin is small.

source: Turney, Littman, Bigham and Shnayder (2003) Combining independent modules to solve multiple-choice synonym and analogy problems (RANLP; arXiv cs/0309035)
finding: First paper to score SAT analogies by corpus phrase vectors. Merged 13 independent modules (WordNet paths, relation tests, dictionary similarity, phrase vectors) with mixture, logarithmic and product rules. Introduced the 374-question SAT set.
numbers: Ensemble on SAT analogies around 43 to 45% with mixture/logarithmic rules (table columns garbled in the PDF text; product rule scored lower in one column). Best single analogy module in the final version was the phrase-vector module. TOEFL synonyms: LSA 43.8% (this run), PMI-IR 69.0%, thesaurus 69.6%, ensemble 80.0 to 82.0% (log rule 82.0%). 374 questions: 90 unofficial prep sites, 14 ETS, 190 from Claman (2000), 80 from guidebooks.
limits: The pdftotext table lost column alignment, so individual ensemble numbers for SAT are approximate; treat the 45% headline as the safe one. This is an early draft where the phrase-vector module was weak.
agent_relevance: An ensemble of heterogeneous modules beat each single one, but the corpus-vector module alone later matched the ensemble. Supports using diverse cheap scorers and combining them by code.

source: Turney (2008) A uniform approach to analogies, synonyms, antonyms, and associations (PairClass; COLING; arXiv 0809.0124)
finding: Recasts SAT analogy, TOEFL synonym, ESL synonym-antonym and similar-vs-associated problems as one supervised word-pair classification. Patterns are mined automatically; an SVM classifies the pair feature vector, with bagged probability estimates.
numbers: SAT 374: 52.1% (only 2 of 12 listed prior systems higher; LRA 56.1). TOEFL 80: 76.2%. ESL 136 synonym-antonym: 75.0% (majority baseline lower). Similar/associated/both 144 pairs: 77.1% (chance 33.3%). Average foreign applicant TOEFL 64.5%.
limits: Needs training labels for each task. SAT here is cross-validated by treating questions as binary pair classification.
agent_relevance: A single pair-vector representation covers many relation judgments. Evidence that one cheap vector store could serve several of the agent's lookups.

source: Turney (2013) Distributional semantics beyond words: supervised learning of analogy and paraphrase, SuperSim (TACL; arXiv 1310.5042)
finding: Builds a 2,245-feature vector from four spaces (log-frequency, PPMI, domain, function) for each analogy quadruple, trains a logistic-regression model on SAT quadruples, and applies it to analogy, noun-modifier composition and SemEval relational ratings.
numbers: SAT five-choice: 54.8% (205/374), statistically indistinguishable from the top ten (51.1 to 57.0%). Ten-choice SAT with asymmetries: 52.7% vs hand-coded dual-space model 47.9% (not significant). SemEval-2012 Task 2 Spearman 0.408 averaged over 69 subcategories: best reported at that date. Seven- and fourteen-choice noun-modifier-to-unigram tasks also tested; PPMI features alone about 59.7% on fourteen-choice; domain space alone 34.6%.
limits: Trained on the same 374 SAT items (cross-validated with the eight quadruples of one question held together). Gains over LRA are within noise.
agent_relevance: Learning a weighted combination of similarity features beats hand tuning with no loss of cheapness. A small learned reranker over cheap features is a sound pattern.

source: Turney and Pantel (2010) From frequency to meaning: vector space models of semantics (JAIR 37; arXiv 1003.1141)
finding: Classifies vector space models into three matrix types: term-document, word-context and pair-pattern. Pair-pattern rows measure relational similarity; word-context rows measure attributional similarity. Argues relational similarity does not reduce to attributional similarity.
numbers: States LRA at 56% vs average US applicant 57% on 374 SAT questions; best attributional 35%; best non-VSM 43% (Veale 2004). Uses mason:stone / carpenter:wood and a mason:glass vs carpenter:clay counter-example.
quote: we can measure relational similarity by the cosine of the angle between rows in a pair-pattern matrix
limits: Review written in 2010, before neural embeddings took over; says nothing on LLM-era results.
agent_relevance: Gives the clean taxonomy: use pair-pattern vectors for relations, word-context vectors for topic. Our retrieval index should separate the two.

source: Mikolov, Chen, Corrado and Dean (2013) Efficient estimation of word representations in vector space (arXiv 1301.3781)
finding: Shows that relations between words appear as constant vector offsets in a word embedding. Answer 'a is to b as c is to ?' by argmax cosine to v(b) - v(a) + v(c), excluding the three input words. Introduces the Semantic-Syntactic Word Relationship test set (8,869 semantic, 10,675 syntactic questions).
numbers: Skip-gram 640-d on 320M words: semantic 55%, syntactic 59%. CBOW 24 / 64; NNLM 23 / 53; RNNLM 9 / 36. CBOW with 600 dims on 783M words, 30k-word vocabulary subset: 50.4% total. Doubling both dimensions and data keeps improving, with diminishing gains.
limits: Benchmark mixes nine easy morphological relations with five semantic ones, mostly one-to-one capital/country style. Later work shows much of this is neighbourhood structure (see a14, a15).
agent_relevance: The neural successor to pair-pattern vectors: a single relation vector is the difference of two word vectors. Cheap, but only reliable for regular lexical relations.

source: Levy and Goldberg (2014) Linguistic regularities in sparse and explicit word representations (CoNLL)
finding: The analogy effect is not special to neural embeddings. Sparse explicit PPMI vectors show it too once the scoring rule is fixed. Introduces 3CosMul (multiplicative objective), which lifts explicit vectors a lot.
numbers: MSR set: 3CosAdd embedding 53.98%, explicit 29.04%; 3CosMul embedding 59.09%, explicit 56.83%. Google set: 3CosAdd embedding 62.70%, explicit 45.05%; 3CosMul embedding 66.72%, explicit 68.24%. Per-category 3CosAdd (embedding vs explicit) capital-common-countries 90.51 vs 99.41; currency 14.55 vs 10.53; adjective-to-adverb 24.29 vs 14.01.
limits: Same datasets as Mikolov. Largest errors are due to the target being a near neighbour of an input word; they attribute 49% of explicit and 39% of embedding errors to a single category pattern.
agent_relevance: Gives a direct line back to Turney's count vectors: the same relational regularities are present in plain PPMI count vectors. Count-based pair vectors are not obsolete; scoring rule matters more than vector type.

source: Linzen (2016) Issues in evaluating semantic spaces using word analogies (arXiv 1606.07736)
finding: The offset method conflates offset consistency with nearest-neighbour structure. A literal implementation fails because the nearest neighbour of b - a + a' is nearly always b. Baselines that ignore the offset do surprisingly well.
numbers: Without excluding inputs: nearest neighbour was b in 93% of cases and a in 5%. Overall accuracy of ADD in three skip-gram spaces: .53 (window 2), .60 (window 5), .58 (window 10). Baseline 'IGNORE-A' reached .41/.29/.36 in some of them; 'ONLY-B' .42/.36/.33. Plurals: ONLY-B alone .70. Reversing analogy direction cut accuracy by 0.11 on average (US cities .69 to .17; common capitals .90 to .53). Category accuracy ranged from .13 to .90.
limits: Three skip-gram spaces on ukWaC plus Wikipedia only; Mikolov sets only.
agent_relevance: A warning: a high analogy score from cheap vectors can come from word neighbourhoods rather than relation structure. Test any relational similarity gate on reversed and distractor items, as G3 requires (pass on something not fitted).

source: Drozd, Gladkova and Matsuoka (2016) Word embeddings, analogies, and machine learning: beyond king - man + woman = queen (COLING)
finding: Linear offset fails for many relations even though the information is present in the embedding. Averaging offsets over several example pairs (3CosAvg) and a classifier-plus-cosine method (LRCos) recover much more.
numbers: Google test: state of the art for 3CosAdd about 65% to 75.6% (GloVe). BATS: GloVe drops from 80.4% on Google to 28.5%. Best 3CosAdd on BATS 28.1% (GloVe), PairDistance 7.5%, 3CosAvg 34.4%, LRCos 47.7% (Skip-Gram), LRCosF 47.2%. Gains of LRCos over 3CosAdd: up to 25 points on encyclopedic, up to 34 on derivational, up to 8 on lexicographic relations. SVD1000 on first test: 3CosAdd 58.1 vs LRCos 74.6.
limits: Uses supervised class information (several example pairs). Accuracy still varies 17 to 28 points between categories.
agent_relevance: Several worked examples of a relation give a better relation vector than one pair. For our agent: retrieve with a set of exemplars of the relation, not one pair.

source: Gladkova, Drozd and Matsuoka (2016) Analogy-based detection of morphological and semantic relations with word embeddings: what works and what doesn't (NAACL SRW; BATS)
finding: Builds BATS, a balanced analogy test set of 99,200 questions in 40 relations across inflection, derivation, lexicography and encyclopedia. Shows that the Google set hid large category differences.
numbers: BATS: 40 relations, 50 pairs each, 2,480 questions per relation, 99,200 total. Mikolov's set has 5 semantic and 9 morphological categories with 20 to 70 pairs. On the Google set, accuracy ranged 10.53% to 99.41% by category; one category was 56.72% of all semantic questions. GloVe 80.4% average on Google (6B tokens: 71.7% in original). SVD model on Google 49.9% here vs 52.6% reported earlier.
limits: Reproduction on a 1.8B-token Wikipedia snapshot. The single-answer scoring can reject valid alternatives.
agent_relevance: Reporting one aggregate analogy score hides huge category spread. Any evaluation of our similarity gate should be reported per relation type.

source: Chen, Peterson and Griffiths (2017) Evaluating vector-space models of analogy (CogSci; arXiv 1705.04416)
finding: Tests the parallelogram model (the cognitive-science model behind word2vec arithmetic) against human relational-similarity ratings. Finds some relation types captured and others not, and finds human judgments violate the geometric constraints of a vector space.
numbers: Human ratings on 5,000+ SemEval-2012 pairs: within-subtype mean 5.01 (SD 1.98), between-subtype 4.02 (SD 2.14), between-type 2.70 (SD 1.93) (scale 1 to 7). Order effect in asymmetric items: 4.76 vs 2.36 depending on presentation order (example comb:pitcher). Triangle-inequality triads: types 1-2 and 2-3 analogies rated 5.44 and 5.43, type 1-3 analogies 2.99; F(2,33)=45.57, p<0.001 while word2vec and GloVe predictions did not differ (F=1.20, p=.31 and F=.24, p=.79). Cosine fits CASE RELATIONS best, fails completely on SIMILAR and CONTRAST.
limits: Mechanical Turk samples; word2vec and GloVe only; comparison of a one-offset-per-pair model, not of pair-pattern models such as LRA.
agent_relevance: Human relational similarity is asymmetric and non-transitive, so no single metric space will match it. Our cheap relation vector should be a recall filter, with a structural check afterward.

source: Brown et al. (2020) Language models are few-shot learners (GPT-3), section 3.9.3 SAT analogies
finding: GPT-3 175B passes the average human SAT-analogy score using a prompt only, with no pair-pattern machinery. Performance rises with in-context examples and with scale.
numbers: 374 SAT questions: zero-shot 53.7%, one-shot 59.1%, few-shot 65.2%; college-applicant average 57%; random 20%. Full 175B model about +10 points over 13B. Appendix H lists 30.5% at the smallest model sizes (zero-shot).
quote: On this task GPT-3 achieves 65.2% in the few-shot setting, 59.1% in the one-shot setting, and 53.7% in the zero-shot setting
limits: SAT questions are public web text, so training-set contamination cannot be excluded; Brown et al. flag no contamination check specific to this set in the section. Few-shot examples came from the same distribution.
agent_relevance: A large LM beats the best 2006 count-vector system (56.1) by 9 points on the same test. The gap that cheap vector similarity needs to close is small; it is not a stand-in for an LLM on hard items.

source: Ushio, Espinosa-Anke, Schockaert and Camacho-Collados (2021) BERT is to NLP what AlexNet is to CV: can pre-trained language models identify analogies? (ACL; arXiv 2105.04949)
finding: Unsupervised scoring of analogies by language-model perplexity (three scoring rules: sPPL, sPMI, smPPL) over SAT, U2, U4 (educational) and Google, BATS. LMs help but struggle with abstract relations; results are very sensitive to prompt template and hyperparameters. Best configs with GPT-2 and RoBERTa; BERT could not beat word embeddings.
numbers: Average accuracy over five datasets (tuned): BERT up to 56.9, GPT-2 up to 66.7, RoBERTa up to 68.1 (SAT 53.7, U2 57.0, U4 55.8, Google 93.6, BATS 80.5 for the best RoBERTa row). Full SAT: LRA 56.4 (their re-listing; paper says 56.8 precision), GPT-3 zero-shot 53.7, few-shot 65.2 (uses examples), FastText about 57.8 on SAT-style row, random 20.0. Best tuned LMs only barely beat LRA. Template ordering a:b::c:d best; permutations mixing the two pairs (a:c::b:d) hurt most. Harder-for-human items also harder for models.
quote: even with optimal hyperparameter values, LMs barely outperform the performance of the simpler LRA model
limits: Table 4 text extraction is jumbled, so SAT-row values for specific models are partial. Hyperparameters tuned on validation split; Google set favours word embeddings.
agent_relevance: LLM perplexity scoring needed careful tuning to pass a 2005 count-vector baseline. Cheap vector scorers remain a competitive reference baseline for any analogy gate.

source: Webb, Holyoak and Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models (Nature Human Behaviour; arXiv 2212.09196)
finding: Zero-shot GPT-3 compared against UCLA undergraduate participants on text-matrix reasoning, letter-string analogies, four-term verbal analogies and story analogies. GPT-3 matched or beat human averages on several, including SAT analogies from Turney et al.
numbers: Digit Matrices: humans N=40; letter-string analogies N=57; verbal analogies N=57; story analogies N=54. GPT-3 above human average on all matrix problem types (odds ratio example 1.88, p=0.005, 95% CI 1.21 to 2.91). SAT set: 374 problems, chance 20%, GPT-3 above the estimated average high-school SAT-taker. Jones et al. set (N=241 humans): GPT-3 in human range but numerically lower.
limits: Training data may include SAT items (they discuss contamination and built new items). Zero-shot with some prompt design. Participants are UCLA undergraduates.
agent_relevance: By 2023 plain LLMs outperform the 2006 text-statistics approach on the same benchmark. Count-vector similarity is useful as cheap retrieval, not as the reasoning step.

source: Turney (2006) Table 15 / 95% intervals and what 'human-level' means
finding: The claim of human-level performance rests on overlap of confidence intervals, not on a direct comparison with a human sample.
numbers: VSM-AV recall 47.1% (CI 42.2 to 52.5, excludes 57%); VSM-WMTS 38.5% (CI 33.5 to 43.6, excludes 57%); LRA 56.1% (CI 51.0 to 61.2, includes 57%). Human mean 57% derived from the College Board percentile of 78 verbal items assuming equal difficulty.
limits: Estimated human number, not measured on these 374 items; the interval for LRA is about +/-5 points.
agent_relevance: Treat 'human-level' claims for cheap similarity as soft. Use own measured baselines on our own items.

source: Turney and Littman (2005) noun-modifier classification with 128-d vectors
finding: Applies the same pair-vector cosine to classify relations between noun and modifier in 600 hand-labelled pairs with single nearest neighbour and leave-one-out cross-validation.
numbers: 30 classes: accuracy 27.8% (167/600), macro F 26.5% vs 3.3% for random; per-class F from 0% (obj, top) to 64.3% (whl) and 62.1% (part). 5 classes: accuracy 45.7% (274/600), F 43.2% vs 20.0%. Threshold on margin of 0.03: precision 35.5%, recall 11.7% (30 classes).
limits: Highly skewed classes of 3 to 49 items. Unexplained improvement in F with negative margin threshold, which the authors call noise.
agent_relevance: Per-class numbers are very uneven. A relation-type vector will be reliable for some relations and blind for others, so keep a per-type reliability table.

source: Turney (2006) manual vs automatic patterns, and why vectors beat rule patterns (sections 6.8 to 6.9)
finding: LRA's 4,000 automatic patterns include nearly all of the 64 hand patterns of Turney and Littman, so the gain is in quantity, not a new kind of pattern. A vector is a distributed representation and holds more than any single Hearst-style pattern.
numbers: 50 of 64 manual patterns appear exactly among automatic patterns; 60 of 64 with wildcard leniency. LRA uses 4,000 patterns, with 128 in the earlier work.
quote: a vector contains more information than any single pattern or small set of patterns; a vector is a distributed representation
limits: Explanation of relation from vectors left as future work.
agent_relevance: Noisy patterns are fine when pooled into a vector, but cannot be used as individual rules. Same logic for pooling weak relation cues in our scaffold.

source: Turney et al. (2003) and Turney (2006): lexicon-based vs corpus-based SAT results across years
finding: Timeline of SAT-analogy accuracy from the paper's related work: Veale (2004) lexicon-based paths over WordNet scored 43%; VSM of Turney and Littman 47%; LRA 56%. The authors suggest combining corpus and lexicon methods.
limits: Same 374 items across years, which invites overfitting of design choices.
agent_relevance: Gives a ladder of cheap-method ceilings (43, 47, 56) to compare to LLM results (54 zero-shot to 65 few-shot).

source: Mikolov, Sutskever, Chen, Corrado and Dean (2013) Distributed representations of words and phrases and their compositionality (arXiv 1310.4546)
finding: Adds negative sampling, subsampling of frequent words and phrase vectors to skip-gram, and shows additive compositionality of vectors on analogies.
numbers: Reports analogical reasoning accuracy for phrase and word tasks (best model 72% on the phrase analogy set, per the paper text).
limits: Only the 72% headline was checked; table values were not.
agent_relevance: Source of the practical word2vec recipe that replaced hand-built count vectors.
